Appendix A Renormalization-group perspective on finite-resource scaling

This appendix summarizes the renormalization-group (RG) arguments underlying the finite-resource scaling analysis used in Section II. The central idea is that finite variational resources act as an effective relevant perturbation of a critical fixed point, generating an emergent correlation length in direct analogy with finite-size and finite-temperature effects. We first briefly review the RG description of critical systems before deriving the corresponding scaling forms.

At a quantum critical point, the long-distance physics is invariant under changes of length scale. The RG [66, 67] provides the formal framework for describing this scale invariance. In the Euclidean path-integral representation, illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the ground state is represented by a two-dimensional spacetime partition function with microscopic spacings aa in space and δ\delta in imaginary time. An RG transformation coarse grains both directions by a scale factor bb,

a\displaystyle a →a′=b​a,\displaystyle\rightarrow a^{\prime}=ba, (42)
δ\displaystyle\delta →δ′=b​δ,\displaystyle\rightarrow\delta^{\prime}=b\delta, (43)

while preserving the long-distance physics. Repeated coarse graining defines a flow in the space of Hamiltonians. Critical Hamiltonians correspond to unstable fixed points of this flow, whereas generic gapped phases flow toward stable trivial fixed points.

The behavior close to a critical fixed point is determined by the scaling operators o^\hat{o}, defined through

o^→o^′=b−Δo​o^,\displaystyle\hat{o}\rightarrow\hat{o}^{\prime}=b^{-\Delta_{o}}\hat{o}, (44)

where Δo\Delta_{o} is the scaling dimension. A perturbation of the Hamiltonian by a local operator,

H=H∗+g​∫o^​dx,\displaystyle H=H^{*}+g\int\hat{o}\differential{x}, (45)

therefore induces the RG flow

g⁡(b)∝bd−Δo,\displaystyle g(b)\propto b^{d-\Delta_{o}}, (46)

where dd is the spacetime dimension. Perturbations with Δo<d\Delta_{o}<d grow under coarse graining and are therefore relevant, while those with Δo>d\Delta_{o}>d are irrelevant. A relevant perturbation drives the system away from the critical fixed point and generates a finite correlation length,

ξ∝g−ν,ν=1d−Δo.\displaystyle\xi\propto g^{-\nu},\qquad\nu=\frac{1}{d-\Delta_{o}}. (47)

The same RG picture provides a natural interpretation of finite-resource variational approximations of critical ground states. Rather than viewing finite circuit depth as a generic approximation error, we regard it as an effective relevant perturbation that displaces the variational state away from the critical fixed point. The finite variational resource therefore induces an emergent correlation length ξD\xi_{D}, analogous to the correlation lengths generated by finite system size or finite temperature. The central hypothesis of this work is that the scaling of ξD\xi_{D} with the available resources provides a universal measure of the expressiveness of a variational ansatz. We now show how this picture naturally recovers the familiar finite-size and finite-temperature scaling forms before extending them to finite-resource scaling.

Finite-size scaling.

A finite system provides the simplest example of an infrared cutoff. For a lattice model with N=L/aN=L/a sites, the RG transformation successively reduces the number of degrees of freedom and can therefore be iterated only until the coarse-grained system contains 𝒪⁡(1)\order{1} sites. Consequently, the total rescaling factor is bounded by

bmax∼La.\displaystyle b_{\max}\sim\frac{L}{a}. (48)

From the RG perspective, this finite cutoff prevents the flow from reaching the critical fixed point. Instead, it is equivalent to introducing an effective relevant perturbation whose strength is set by the largest accessible length scale,

geff∝bmax−(d−Δo)∝(La)−1/ν,\displaystyle g_{\mathrm{eff}}\propto b_{\max}^{-(d-\Delta_{o})}\propto\left(\frac{L}{a}\right)^{-1/\nu}, (49)

where we used Eq. (46). The corresponding correlation length is therefore limited by the system size,

ξL∝geff−ν∝L.\displaystyle\xi_{L}\propto g_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-\nu}\propto L. (50)

The finite critical system is thus equivalent, within the scaling regime, to an infinite system perturbed away from criticality by a coupling geff∼L−1/νg_{\mathrm{eff}}\sim L^{-1/\nu}. Universal observables consequently depend only on the ratio between the two infrared length scales, L/ξ⁡(g)L/\xi(g), leading to the familiar finite-size scaling forms discussed in the main text.

Finite-temperature scaling.

Finite temperature provides a second example of an infrared cutoff. In the Euclidean path-integral representation, illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the imaginary-time direction has a finite extent β\beta, so the RG flow is truncated once the coarse-grained temporal dimension reaches 𝒪⁡(1)\order{1}. This introduces the thermal correlation length

ξβ=v​β1/z,\displaystyle\xi_{\beta}=v\,\beta^{1/z}, (51)

where vv is the velocity of the low-energy excitations and zz the dynamical critical exponent. When ξβ<L\xi_{\beta}<L, thermal fluctuations dominate the infrared physics, and universal observables depend on the two dimensionless ratios L/ξ⁡(g)L/\xi(g) and L/ξβL/\xi_{\beta}, leading to the standard finite-temperature scaling forms.

Finite-resource scaling.

Finite variational resources provide a third infrared cutoff. The central hypothesis of this work is that a finite-depth parameterized quantum evolution can be interpreted as an effective relevant perturbation of the critical fixed point. Consequently, the finite resource induces an emergent correlation length ξD\xi_{D}, which truncates the RG flow in exactly the same way as the finite system size or the finite temperature.

Universal observables therefore depend only on the ratios between the three competing infrared scales, LL, ξβ\xi_{\beta}, and ξD\xi_{D}, together with the correlation length ξ⁡(g)\xi(g) associated with deviations from criticality. Restricting to zero temperature leaves the two-scale problem discussed in the main text, where observables become universal functions of L/ξDL/\xi_{D}. The limiting regimes ξD≫L\xi_{D}\gg L and ξD≪L\xi_{D}\ll L, together with the scaling forms used to extract the exponent κ\kappa, are discussed in Section II.2.

Appendix B Optimization procedure

This appendix summarizes the optimization procedure used throughout this work. All variational states are optimized by imaginary-time evolution projected onto the variational manifold using the quantum natural gradient. Since both the target Hamiltonian and all variational generators are quadratic fermionic operators, every quantity entering the optimization, including the energy, its gradient, and the Fubini–Study metric, can be evaluated exactly within the fermionic Gaussian formalism. We first briefly review the natural-gradient equations in Section B.1 before describing their efficient implementation for free Gaussian fermionic models in Section B.2.

B.1 Natural-gradient optimization

Any variational ansatz defines a manifold of quantum states parameterized by a set of variational parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta},

M={|ψ⁡(𝜽)⟩}.\displaystyle M=\{\ket{\psi(\bm{\theta})}\}\,. (52)

To optimize these parameters we employ variational imaginary-time evolution based on the McLachlan variational principle [101, 102]. The exact imaginary-time evolution of the density matrix,

∂ρ∂τ=−{H,ρ}+2​⟨H⟩ρ​ρ≕ℒ⁡[ρ],\displaystyle\partialderivative{\rho}{\tau}=-\anticommutator{H}{\rho}+2\expectationvalue{H}_{\rho}\,\rho\eqqcolon\mathcal{L}[\rho], (53)

is projected onto the tangent space of the variational manifold by minimizing the distance between the exact evolution and its variational approximation.

The McLachlan variational principle determines the parameter velocities by minimizing the distance between the exact and variational imaginary-time evolution,

‖∑n∂ρ∂θn​∂θn∂τ−ℒ⁡[ρ]‖2.\displaystyle\norm{ \sum_n \pdv{\rho}{\theta_n} \pdv{\theta_n}{\tau} - \mathcal{L}[\rho] }^{2}. (54)

This projection yields the variational imaginary-time evolution equation

2​∑mgn​m​∂θm∂τ=Tr⁡(∂ρ∂θn​ℒ​[ρ]),\displaystyle 2\sum_{m}g_{nm}\partialderivative{\theta_m}{\tau}=\Tr( \pdv{\rho}{\theta_n} \mathcal{L}[\rho] ), (55)

where gn​mg_{nm} is the Fubini–Study metric on the variational manifold. For pure states, the Fubini–Study metric is given by

gn​m\displaystyle g_{nm} =Re(Gn​m),\displaystyle=\real(G_{nm}), (56)
Gn​m\displaystyle G_{nm} =⟨∂ψ∂θn|∂ψ∂θm⟩−⟨∂ψ∂θn|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|∂ψ∂θm⟩\displaystyle=\innerproduct{\pdv{\psi}{\theta_n}}{\pdv{\psi}{\theta_m}}-\innerproduct{\pdv{\psi}{\theta_n}}{\psi}\innerproduct{\psi}{\pdv{\psi}{\theta_m}}
=In​m4,\displaystyle=\frac{I_{nm}}{4}, (57)

where In​mI_{nm} denotes the quantum Fisher information matrix. For pure states, the right-hand side of Eq. (55) reduces to the energy gradient,

Tr⁡(∂ρ∂θn​ℒ​[ρ])=−∂⟨H⟩∂θn,\displaystyle\Tr( \pdv{\rho}{\theta_n} \mathcal{L}[\rho] )=-\partialderivative{\expval{H}}{\theta_n}, (58)

so that the optimization corresponds to an imaginary-time natural-gradient flow toward a stationary point of the variational energy. Rather than discretizing Eq. (55) with a fixed-step Euler scheme, we integrate it using an adaptive Dormand–Prince fourth/fifth-order Runge–Kutta method [103, 104], which provides improved numerical stability and convergence. In practice, this natural-gradient integration acts as a strong preconditioner: the Fubini–Study metric rescales the descent direction according to the local geometry of the manifold and carries the state rapidly through the bulk of the optimization landscape. The final approach to the local minimum is markedly slower, because the metric becomes increasingly flat in this region and the natural-gradient direction loses much of its advantage. An adaptive line search along the update direction mitigates this slowdown, but such schemes are constructed for near-Euclidean geometries. We therefore complete the last, short segment of the trajectory using a plain Euclidean gradient descent. This is justified because any smooth manifold is locally flat. Over the small remaining parameter distance the Fubini–Study metric is effectively constant, so the natural and Euclidean gradients differ only by a fixed linear rescaling and share the same stationary points. The Euclidean gradient therefore provides a valid and inexpensive descent direction for the final convergence.

B.2 Efficient implementation for fermionic Gaussian states

The optimization described above becomes numerically efficient because both the target Hamiltonian and all variational generators considered in this work are quadratic fermionic operators. Consequently, every variational state remains a fermionic Gaussian state throughout the evolution and can be represented exactly by its correlation matrix. This avoids the exponential growth of the Hilbert space and enables exact evaluation of the energy, its gradients, and the Fubini–Study metric for systems containing several hundred sites. In this section we summarize the Gaussian formalism underlying our implementation, following the notation of Ref. [92].

A fermionic Gaussian state on a lattice with NN sites is completely characterized by its two-point correlation functions. We collect them into the Dirac correlation matrix

Γ=(⟨cn†​cm⟩⟨cn†​cm†⟩⟨cn​cm⟩⟨cn​cm†⟩),\displaystyle\Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}\expectationvalue{c_n^\dagger c_m}&\expectationvalue{c_n^\dagger c_m^\dagger}\\ \expectationvalue{c_n c_m}&\expectationvalue{c_n c_m^\dagger}\end{pmatrix}, (59)

written in the Nambu basis. Likewise, every quadratic Hamiltonian admits the Bogoliubov–de Gennes representation

H=∑n,m=1N\displaystyle H=\sum_{n,m=1}^{N} (An,m​cn†​cm−An,m∗​cn​cm†CLOSE\displaystyle\big(A_{n,m}c^{\dagger}_{n}c_{m}-A^{*}_{n,m}c_{n}c^{\dagger}_{m}
OPEN+Bn,m​cn​cm−Bn,m∗​cn†​cm†),\displaystyle+B_{n,m}c_{n}c_{m}-B^{*}_{n,m}c^{\dagger}_{n}c^{\dagger}_{m}\big)\,, (60)

where A=A†A=A^{\dagger}, and BT=−BB^{T}=-B. Representing both states and generators in the Bogoliubov–de Gennes form allows every layer unitary to be evaluated efficiently through the eigendecomposition of its single-particle Hamiltonian. This is particularly important for the combined ansätze introduced in Section IV.2, where a layer is generated by a linear combination of non-commuting operators,

hs=∑kθs,k​Gs,k,\displaystyle h_{s}=\sum_{k}\theta_{s,k}G_{s,k}, (61)

so that the derivative of the corresponding unitary cannot be obtained by differentiating each exponential separately. Instead, it requires the Fréchet derivative of the matrix exponential.

Writing the eigendecomposition of the layer Hamiltonian as

hs=Vs​Ds​Vs†,\displaystyle h_{s}=V_{s}D_{s}V_{s}^{\dagger}, (62)

with

Ds=diag⁡(d1,…,d2​N),\displaystyle D_{s}=\mathrm{diag}(d_{1},\ldots,d_{2N}), (63)

the layer propagator is

Us=exp⁡(−i​hs).\displaystyle U_{s}=\exp(-\i h_s). (64)

Denoting matrices expressed in the eigenbasis of hsh_{s} by

A~=Vs†​A​Vs,\displaystyle\widetilde{A}=V_{s}^{\dagger}AV_{s}, (65)

the derivative of the propagator with respect to the parameter θs,k\theta_{s,k} is given exactly by Duhamel’s formula,

∂Us∂θs,k\displaystyle\partialderivative{U_s}{\theta_{s,k}} =−i∫01e−i⁡(1−τ)​hsGs,ke−i​τ​hsdτ\displaystyle=-\mathrm{i}\int_{0}^{1}e^{-\mathrm{i}(1-\tau)h_{s}}G_{s,k}e^{-\mathrm{i}\tau h_{s}}\,d\tau
=−i​Vs​(Φs−⊙G~s,k)​Vs†,\displaystyle=-\mathrm{i}V_{s}\left(\Phi_{s}^{-}\odot\widetilde{G}_{s,k}\right)V_{s}^{\dagger}, (66)

where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication and the Fréchet kernel Φs−\Phi_{s}^{-} is the divided difference of the negative exponential,

(Φs−)m​n={e−i​dm−e−i​dn−i⁡(dm−dn),m≠n,e−i​dm,m=n.\displaystyle\left(\Phi_{s}^{-}\right)_{mn}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{e^{-\mathrm{i}d_{m}}-e^{-\mathrm{i}d_{n}}}{-\mathrm{i}(d_{m}-d_{n})},&m\neq n,\\[10.00002pt] e^{-\mathrm{i}d_{m}},&m=n.\end{cases} (67)

It is useful to introduce the Hermitian tangent generator at the output of layer ss,

Ks,k\displaystyle K_{s,k} =i​∂Us∂θs,k​Us†\displaystyle=\mathrm{i}\partialderivative{U_s}{\theta_{s,k}}U_{s}^{\dagger}
=Vs​[(Φs−⊙G~s,k)​ei​Ds]​Vs†.\displaystyle=V_{s}\left[\left(\Phi_{s}^{-}\odot\widetilde{G}_{s,k}\right)e^{\mathrm{i}D_{s}}\right]V_{s}^{\dagger}. (68)

Thus, once the eigendecomposition of hsh_{s} has been computed, both the layer propagator and all of its tangent generators are obtained exactly without numerical differentiation.

The availability of the layer propagators and their Fréchet derivatives enables an efficient implementation of the natural-gradient optimization. Rather than differentiating the full circuit repeatedly, the energy, its gradient, and the Fubini–Study metric are all obtained through a single forward/backward sweep over the variational circuit. The forward sweep propagates the correlation matrix through the layers, while the backward sweep propagates an adjoint matrix encoding the derivative of the energy with respect to the intermediate correlation matrices.

Forward sweep.

Starting from the initial correlation matrix Γ0\Gamma_{0}, each variational layer acts by a Bogoliubov transformation,

Γs=Us​Γs−1​Us†,Us=e−i​hs,\displaystyle\Gamma_{s}=U_{s}\Gamma_{s-1}U_{s}^{\dagger},\qquad U_{s}=e^{-\mathrm{i}h_{s}}, (69)

where hsh_{s} is the Bogoliubov–de Gennes matrix generating layer ss. During the forward sweep we store the intermediate correlation matrices together with the eigendecompositions of each layer Hamiltonian. These quantities are subsequently reused in the gradient and metric evaluation, avoiding repeated diagonalizations.

Energy evaluation.

For a quadratic target Hamiltonian, the variational energy is linear in the correlation matrix and can therefore be written as

ℓ⁡(𝜽)=Tr⁡(Λ0​ΓD),\displaystyle\ell(\bm{\theta})=\Tr(\Lambda_0\Gamma_D), (70)

where Λ0\Lambda_{0} is determined solely by the target Hamiltonian. This linear form makes the subsequent adjoint evaluation particularly efficient.

Backward sweep: adjoint gradient.

We define the adjoint cost matrix Λs\Lambda_{s} by back-propagating Λ0\Lambda_{0} through the same layer unitaries,

Λs−1=Us†​Λs​Us.\displaystyle\Lambda_{s-1}=U_{s}^{\dagger}\,\Lambda_{s}\,U_{s}. (71)

The energy gradient with respect to a parameter θs,k\theta_{s,k} of layer ss is then a single trace evaluated at stage ss. Since ∂θs,kΓs=−i​[Ks,k,Γs]\partial_{\theta_{s,k}}\Gamma_{s}=-\mathrm{i}\commutator{K_{s,k}}{\Gamma_s}, it reads

∂ℓ∂θs,k\displaystyle\partialderivative{\ell}{\theta_{s,k}} =−i​Tr⁡(Λs​[Ks,k,Γs])\displaystyle=-\mathrm{i}\Tr\left(\Lambda_{s}\commutator{K_{s,k}}{\Gamma_s}\right)
=2​ℑ​𝔪​Tr⁡[Λ~s​(Φs−⊙G~s,k)​Γ~s−1​ei​Ds],\displaystyle=2\,\mathfrak{Im}\,\Tr\left[\widetilde{\Lambda}_{s}\left(\Phi_{s}^{-}\odot\widetilde{G}_{s,k}\right)\widetilde{\Gamma}_{s-1}e^{\mathrm{i}D_{s}}\right], (72)

where the tildes denote rotation into the eigenbasis of hsh_{s}, A~=Vs†​A​Vs\widetilde{A}=V_{s}^{\dagger}A\,V_{s}. In a separable layer, hs=θs,k​Gs,kh_{s}=\theta_{s,k}G_{s,k}, so Gs,kG_{s,k} commutes with hsh_{s} and Eq. 68 reduces to Ks,k=Gs,kK_{s,k}=G_{s,k}. Consequently,

∂ℓ∂θs,k=−i​Tr⁡(Λs​[Gs,k,Γs]),\displaystyle\partialderivative{\ell}{\theta_{s,k}}=-\mathrm{i}\Tr\left(\Lambda_{s}\commutator{G_{s,k}}{\Gamma_s}\right), (73)

which is the familiar commutator form for a unitary derivative. Thus, once the forward sweep has been completed, every variational parameter contributes only a single trace evaluation, yielding the complete energy gradient without finite-difference approximations.

Fubini–Study metric.

The same forward sweep yields the Fubini–Study metric tensor gk​lg_{kl} of Eq. 56. Using Wick’s theorem in the Nambu-doubled convention above, the entry coupling parameters kk and ll (with sk≤sls_{k}\leq s_{l}) is

gk​l=12​ℜ​𝔢​Tr⁡[Ksk,k​Γsk​Ksl,l(l→sk)​(𝕀−Γsk)],\displaystyle g_{kl}=\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{Re}\Tr\left[K_{s_{k},k}\Gamma_{s_{k}}K_{s_{l},l}^{(l\to s_{k})}\left(\mathbb{I}-\Gamma_{s_{k}}\right)\right], (74)

where

Ksl,l(l→sk)=Usk+1†⋯Usl†Ksl,lUsl⋯Usk+1\displaystyle K_{s_{l},l}^{(l\to s_{k})}=U_{s_{k}+1}^{\dagger}\cdots U_{s_{l}}^{\dagger}K_{s_{l},l}U_{s_{l}}\cdots U_{s_{k}+1} (75)

is the tangent generator of parameter ll, including its within-layer Fréchet dressing, backward-evolved in the Heisenberg picture to the output of layer sks_{k}. The entries for sl<sks_{l}<s_{k} follow from the symmetry gk​l=gl​kg_{kl}=g_{lk}.

The forward and backward sweeps therefore provide the energy, its gradient, and the Fubini–Study metric simultaneously, so that each optimization step requires only a single traversal of the circuit.

B.3 Optimized variational parameters

As an illustration of the optimization procedure described above, Fig. 5 shows the optimized variational parameters obtained after convergence for all ansätze at the representative system size L=128​aL=128a. Beyond providing a concrete example of the parameter profiles produced by the natural-gradient optimization, these results also support an important methodological assumption of this work. Across all ansätze, the optimized parameters remain bounded as the circuit depth increases, rather than growing systematically with DD. This indicates that the increased expressiveness of the variational state is primarily achieved through the addition of layers, rather than through increasingly large parameter values, supporting the use of the circuit depth DD as the relevant measure of computational resources throughout the scaling analysis.

Appendix C Conformal perturbation theory modeling the VQE state

This appendix derives the effective scaling forms used to analyze the numerical results of Section IV.3. Following the scaling hypothesis described in Section II, we model a finite-depth variational state as the ground state of an effective Hamiltonian

H=HT+g​V,\displaystyle H=H_{T}+gV, (76)

where HTH_{T} is the critical target Hamiltonian and V=∫0LΦ⁡(x)​dxV=\int_{0}^{L}\Phi(x)\,\differential x is the leading symmetry-allowed perturbation. This effective description predicts both the exponential cutoff of correlation functions used to extract the finite-depth correlation length ξD\xi_{D}, and the finite-depth scaling of the variational energy. Throughout this appendix, |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} denotes the optimized variational state, |Ω⟩\ket{\Omega} the ground state of HTH_{T}, and E0​(L)E_{0}(L) its finite-size ground-state energy.

C.1 Correlation functions

We first derive the observable used to extract the finite-depth correlation length, namely the longitudinal spin–spin correlation function

Cx​x​(m,n)=⟨σmx​σnx⟩.\displaystyle C_{xx}(m,n)=\expectationvalue{\sigma^x_m\sigma^x_n}. (77)

For the transverse-field Ising chain, the Jordan–Wigner transformation maps the spin operators to Majorana strings,

σmx​σnx\displaystyle\sigma^{x}_{m}\sigma^{x}_{n} =BmAm+1Bm+1Am+2⋯Bn−1An,\displaystyle=B_{m}A_{m+1}B_{m+1}A_{m+2}\cdots B_{n-1}A_{n}, (78)
Al\displaystyle A_{l} =cl+cl†,Bl=cl−cl†,\displaystyle=c_{l}+c_{l}^{\dagger},\qquad B_{l}=c_{l}-c_{l}^{\dagger}, (79)

for m<nm<n [87]. For a Gaussian (free-fermion) state, completely characterized by its correlation matrix Γ\Gamma, Wick’s theorem reduces the expectation value of this Majorana string to a Pfaffian which, for the present block structure, simplifies to the determinant of the |n−m|×|n−m|\absolutevalue{n-m}\times\absolutevalue{n-m} matrix of elementary contractions,

f⁡(k,l)\displaystyle f(k,l) ≔⟨Bk​Al⟩\displaystyle\coloneqq\expectationvalue{B_kA_l}
=Γk+N,l−Γk,l+Γk+N,l+N−Γk,l+N,\displaystyle=\Gamma_{k+N,l}-\Gamma_{k,l}+\Gamma_{k+N,l+N}-\Gamma_{k,l+N}, (80)

where the four terms correspond to the correlators ⟨ck​cl⟩\expectationvalue*{c_k c_l}, ⟨ck†​cl⟩\expectationvalue*{c_k^\dagger c_l}, ⟨ck​cl†⟩\expectationvalue*{c_k c_l^\dagger}, and ⟨ck†​cl†⟩\expectationvalue*{c_k^\dagger c_l^\dagger}. The lattice correlator therefore becomes

Cx​x​(m,n)=det⁡[f⁡(m+j−1,m+l)]j,l=1|n−m|,\displaystyle C_{xx}(m,n)=\det[f(m+j-1,m+l)]_{j,l=1}^{\absolutevalue{n-m}}, (81)

with the convention Cx​x​(m,m)=1C_{xx}(m,m)=1. Throughout our numerical calculations, one operator is fixed at the center of the chain while the second is displaced by a distance r=|m−n|r=\absolutevalue{m-n}. Equation (81) therefore provides the exact lattice correlator against which the continuum scaling form is compared.

At criticality, the lattice two-point correlator approaches the conformal field theory prediction for the Ising order parameter, whose scaling dimension is Δσ=1/8\Delta_{\sigma}=1/8. Given one field anchored on the center site and the other a distance rr away with r<Lr<L, the scaling form is given by

Cx​x∞​(r)≃𝒵σ​[Lπ​sin⁡(π​rL)]−2​Δσ,\displaystyle C_{xx}^{\infty}(r)\simeq\mathcal{Z}_{\sigma}\left[\frac{L}{\pi}\sin(\frac{\pi r}{L})\right]^{-2\Delta_{\sigma}}, (82)

where the chord distance

dchord​(r,L)=Lπ​sin⁡(π​rL)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{chord}}(r,L)=\frac{L}{\pi}\sin(\frac{\pi r}{L}) (83)

implements the conformal mapping from the finite interval to the bulk power law, reducing to rr when r≪Lr\ll L, recovering Cx​x∝r−1/4C_{xx}\propto r^{-1/4}.

A finite variational depth introduces an infrared cutoff through the emergent correlation length ξD\xi_{D}. Accordingly, we model the lattice correlator by multiplying the critical conformal prediction by an exponential envelope,

Cx​xD​(r)≃𝒵σ​[Lπ​sin⁡(π​rL)]−2​Δσ​exp(−r/ξD),\displaystyle C_{xx}^{D}(r)\simeq\mathcal{Z}_{\sigma}\left[\frac{L}{\pi}\sin(\frac{\pi r}{L})\right]^{-2\Delta_{\sigma}}\exp(-r/\xi_D), (84)

valid within the scaling window

aX​X≪r≪Landr/ξD≳𝒪⁡(1),\displaystyle a_{XX}\ll r\ll L\quad\text{and}\quad r/\xi_{D}\gtrsim\order{1}, (85)

where aX​Xa_{XX} denotes a non-universal ultraviolet cutoff below which lattice corrections become important. The exponential envelope is the observable manifestation of the effective relevant perturbation introduced in the main text: finite variational resources generate a finite infrared length scale ξD\xi_{D} exactly as a physical perturbation away from criticality would. Consequently, multiplying the measured correlator by the appropriate power of the chord distance removes the universal conformal power law and isolates the exponential decay used in Sec. IV.3 to extract ξD\xi_{D}. The ultraviolet cutoff only affects the non-universal amplitude and short-distance corrections, and therefore does not modify the extracted correlation length.

C.2 Energy shift

We now derive the finite-depth scaling of the variational energy error used in the main text. The observable of interest in this section is the absolute variational energy error,

δ​Eabs=⟨ψ|HT|ψ⟩−E0​(L),\displaystyle\delta E_{\rm abs}=\expectationvalue{H_T}{\psi}-E_{0}(L), (86)

where E0​(L)E_{0}(L) is the exact finite-size ground-state energy of the target Hamiltonian.

Because |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a variational optimum, the energy is stationary with respect to infinitesimal changes of the perturbation strength. Consequently, the linear correction vanishes,

∂δ​Eabs∂g|g=0=0,\displaystyle\evaluated{\pdv{\delta E_{\rm abs}}{g}}_{g=0}=0, (87)

and the leading contribution is quadratic,

δ​Eabs=g2​χm+𝒪⁡(g3),\displaystyle\delta E_{\rm abs}=g^{2}\chi_{m}+\order{g^3}, (88)

where

χm=∑n>0|⟨n|V|Ω⟩|2En−E0\displaystyle\chi_{m}=\sum_{n>0}\frac{\absolutevalue{\mel{n}{V}{\Omega}}^{2}}{E_{n}-E_{0}} (89)

is the generalized susceptibility associated with the perturbation VV.

Using the spectral representation,

1En−E0=∫0∞e−(En−E0)​τ​dτ,\displaystyle\frac{1}{E_{n}-E_{0}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-(E_{n}-E_{0})\tau}\,\differential\tau, (90)

the susceptibility becomes an integrated Euclidean correlation function,

χm=∫0∞⟨W⁡(τ)​W​(0)⟩C​dτ,\displaystyle\chi_{m}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\expectationvalue{W(\tau)W(0)}_{C}\,\differential\tau, (91)

with

W⁡(τ)=e(HT−E0)​τ​V​e−(HT−E0)​τ.\displaystyle W(\tau)=e^{(H_{T}-E_{0})\tau}Ve^{-(H_{T}-E_{0})\tau}. (92)

The perturbation VV contains a spatial integral of the local scaling operator Φ\Phi. In order to progress, we compute the leading bulk contribution by performing the spatial integration explicitly, which would have been possible with true translational invariance,

χm≃L​∫G⁡(u,τ)​du​dτ,\displaystyle\chi_{m}\simeq L\int G(u,\tau)\,\differential u\,\differential\tau, (93)

where

G⁡(u,τ)=⟨Φ⁡(u,τ)​Φ​(0,0)⟩C.\displaystyle G(u,\tau)=\expectationvalue{\Phi(u,\tau)\Phi(0,0)}_{C}. (94)

Within conformal perturbation theory, the connected correlator is approximated by its continuum critical form,

G⁡(r)∝r−2​ΔΦ,\displaystyle G(r)\propto r^{-2\Delta_{\Phi}}, (95)

between a non-universal ultraviolet cutoff aEa_{E} and an infrared cutoff

R≃min⁡(L,ξ).\displaystyle R\simeq\min(L,\xi). (96)

The susceptibility therefore scales as

χm\displaystyle\chi_{m} ∝L​∫aERr1−2​ΔΦ​dr.\displaystyle\propto L\int_{a_{E}}^{R}r^{1-2\Delta_{\Phi}}\,\differential r. (97)

For a relevant perturbation with ΔΦ≤1\Delta_{\Phi}\leq 1,

χm∝L​R2−2​ΔΦ−aE2−2​ΔΦ2−2​ΔΦ,\displaystyle\chi_{m}\propto L\frac{R^{2-2\Delta_{\Phi}}-a_{E}^{2-2\Delta_{\Phi}}}{2-2\Delta_{\Phi}}, (98)

while the borderline case ΔΦ=1\Delta_{\Phi}=1 gives the logarithmic behavior

χm∝L​ln⁡(R/aE).\displaystyle\chi_{m}\propto L\ln(R/a_E). (99)

In the finite-depth regime, ξ≪L\xi\ll L, the infrared cutoff is set by the correlation length, R=ξR=\xi. Since the running coupling is of order unity at this scale, the leading contribution becomes

L​δ​Eabs∝(Lξ)2,\displaystyle L\,\delta E_{\rm abs}\propto\left(\frac{L}{\xi}\right)^{2}, (100)

up to the logarithmic factor

ln⁡(ξ/aE)\displaystyle\ln(\xi/a_E) (101)

for the marginal Ising energy operator with ΔΦ=1\Delta_{\Phi}=1. This is the scaling form used throughout the main text.

The previous result describes the scaling of the total energy correction. For the numerical analysis it is more convenient to isolate the bulk contribution by subtracting the known finite-size CFT correction of the critical Hamiltonian. We therefore define

δ​ebulk=E⁡(L,D)L−e0−eboundaryL,\displaystyle\delta e_{\mathrm{bulk}}=\frac{E(L,D)}{L}-e_{0}-\frac{e_{\mathrm{boundary}}}{L}, (102)

where e0e_{0} and eboundarye_{\mathrm{boundary}} are the bulk and boundary energy densities of the target model. Using the finite-size expansion of the exact critical ground-state energy,

E0​(L)=L​e0+eboundary−π​c​v24​L+𝒪⁡(L−2),\displaystyle E_{0}(L)=Le_{0}+e_{\mathrm{boundary}}-\frac{\pi cv}{24L}+\order{L^{-2}}, (103)

one obtains

L2​δ​ebulk=L​δ​Eabs−π​c​v24+𝒪⁡(L−1).\displaystyle L^{2}\delta e_{\mathrm{bulk}}=L\,\delta E_{\mathrm{abs}}-\frac{\pi cv}{24}+\order{L^{-1}}. (104)

In the finite-depth regime, inserting the conformal perturbation result above gives

L2​δ​ebulk≃B​(Lξ)2​ln⁡(ξaE)−π​c​v24,\displaystyle L^{2}\delta e_{\mathrm{bulk}}\simeq B\left(\frac{L}{\xi}\right)^{2}\ln(\frac{\xi}{a_E})-\frac{\pi cv}{24}, (105)

where BB is a non-universal amplitude. Away from the marginal case, the logarithmic factor is absent.

C.2.1 Jackknife uncertainty estimate

To quantify the stability of the extracted exponent with respect to the limited set of available circuit depths, we use a delete-one-depth jackknife resampling [105]: For nDn_{D} fitted depths, we repeat the complete fit nDn_{D} times, each time omitting all data associated with one depth. If κ(−i)\kappa_{(-i)} denotes the estimate obtained after removing depth DiD_{i} and κ¯(−)=nD−1​∑iκ(−i)\overline{\kappa}_{(-)}=n_{D}^{-1}\sum_{i}\kappa_{(-i)}, the reported jackknife standard error is

σJK=nD−1nD​∑i=1nD(κ(−i)−κ¯(−))2.\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{JK}}=\sqrt{\frac{n_{D}-1}{n_{D}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{D}}\left(\kappa_{(-i)}-\overline{\kappa}_{(-)}\right)^{2}}. (106)

We jackknife resample over depths DD, rather than individual (L,D)(L,D) points, because the scaling exponent κ\kappa is determined by the variation with DD and all system sizes at a given depth share the same leverage on that scaling. In contrast, the standard error obtained from the local curvature of a single least-squares fit is conditional on the selected data and scaling model and can therefore be misleadingly small when only a few depths constrain the exponent. In the present data, the fitted exponent can change appreciably when one depth is removed. Consequently, the jackknife error is the more relevant measure because it exposes this sensitivity directly. It should, however, be interpreted as a diagnostic on fit stability rather than a complete statistical or systematic uncertainty. In particular, when only a few depths are available, neither a small formal fit error nor the jackknife standard error establishes that the asymptotic scaling regime has been reached. Instead, strong variation under leave-one-depth-out resampling signals that additional depths or larger system sizes are required for a well-grounded estimate.

C.2.2 Variable projection fit with the logarithmic correction

Using the finite-depth scaling hypothesis,

ξ=Aξ​Dκ,\displaystyle\xi=A_{\xi}D^{\kappa}, (107)

the energy-shift scaling derived above becomes

y⁡(L,D)\displaystyle y(L,D) ≔L​δ​Eabs​(L,D)\displaystyle\coloneqq L\,\delta E_{\mathrm{abs}}(L,D)
=P​L2​D−2​κ​(κ​ln⁡D+Q),\displaystyle=P\,L^{2}D^{-2\kappa}\left(\kappa\ln D+Q\right), (108)

where P∝B/Aξ2P\propto B/A_{\xi}^{2} is a non-universal amplitude and

Q=ln⁡(Aξ/aE)\displaystyle Q=\ln(A_\xi/a_E) (109)

contains the ultraviolet cutoff introduced by the continuum approximation.

For fixed values of κ\kappa and QQ, Eq. (108) is linear in the amplitude PP. We therefore use a variable-projection procedure [106]: at each trial value of κ\kappa, we scan QQ over its physically allowed interval and determine the optimal PP analytically by weighted linear least squares. The residual minimized by the outer one-dimensional optimization over κ\kappa is thus already profiled over both PP and QQ. To avoid the largest system sizes dominating the fit through the overall L2L^{2} prefactor, we use relative least-squares weights w∝y−2w\propto y^{-2}.

A direct nonlinear fit of all parameters is numerically unstable because the logarithmic term κ​ln⁡D\kappa\ln D and the constant QQ become nearly collinear over the accessible depth window. Consequently, changes in QQ can partially compensate changes in κ\kappa, leading to poorly conditioned fits. We regularize this degeneracy by constraining QQ through its physical interpretation as the ultraviolet cutoff. Since the cutoff satisfies

1≤aE≤ξ⁡(Dmin),\displaystyle 1\leq a_{E}\leq\xi(D_{\min}), (110)

the allowed range becomes

−κ​ln⁡Dmin≤Q≤ln⁡Aξ,\displaystyle-\kappa\ln D_{\min}\leq Q\leq\ln A_{\xi}, (111)

where both AξA_{\xi} and DminD_{\min} are obtained independently from the correlation-length analysis of Appendix C.1. For every admissible QQ at fixed κ\kappa, the amplitude PP is projected out analytically; the value of QQ yielding the smallest weighted residual defines the profiled residual used in the outer optimization over κ\kappa. This procedure stabilizes the extraction of the scaling exponent, while the fitted cutoff itself remains comparatively uncertain because of the residual correlation between QQ and κ\kappa. Once the fit is completed, the corresponding ultraviolet cutoff is recovered from

aE=Aξ​e−Q.\displaystyle a_{E}=A_{\xi}e^{-Q}. (112)

Appendix D Complete scaling analysis for all variational ansätze

For the TFIM HVA, the complete scaling analysis is presented in the main text. Here we collect the corresponding analyses for all remaining variational ansätze considered in this work. Each figure follows the same workflow: extraction of the finite-depth correlation length from the spin correlator, determination of the scaling exponent from the energy-collapse analysis, and quasiparticle occupations in the eigenbasis of the target Hamiltonian. These data underlie the scaling exponents summarized in Table 1 and enable a direct comparison of the different variational architectures at the level of the raw (L,D)(L,D) data.

For the TFIM combined and Kitaev combined ansätze, the shallowest circuit depths do not yet lie in the asymptotic finite-depth scaling regime. This is apparent from the energy-collapse analysis, where these data do not approach the same asymptotic plateau as the deeper circuits. Accordingly, the D=1D=1 data for the TFIM combined ansatz and the D=1,2D=1,2 data for the Kitaev combined ansatz are excluded from the extraction of the scaling exponent reported in Table 1.
